title: MiLTL: A Cross-Modal Contradiction Cascade for On-Device Voice-Phishing Detection
content: Voice phishing (vishing) causes massive financial and psychological harm worldwide, yet the detectors deployed against it are more fragile than their benchmark scores suggest. Systems that transcribe a call and scan it for scam vocabulary look near-perfect on standard Korean corpora, but that success is memorized: when a scammer rephrases the script—or rewrites it with a language model—accuracy collapses, while cloud transcription erodes privacy. We argue that manipulation should be caught by how a call is delivered, not which words it uses. We first build KorMMP, a benchmark that breaks this vocabulary shortcut: it keeps real regulator-sourced scam audio and real benign speech, then decorrelates the transcript from the label, so a keyword matcher cannot win. On it we present MiLTL, an on-device detector that reads a call in short segments through affective and neutrosophic voice channels—centered on a cross-modal contradiction signal that fires when warm words are spoken in a cold, controlling voice, a mismatch that text- and audio-only systems cannot see. A lightweight deterministic stage—an integer-weighted rule carrying zero learned parameters at inference—screens every segment and escalates only the calls that remain ambiguous to a small on-device language model, keeping the algorithm within a resource-constrained edge budget. Trained with the hard benchmark held out, MiLTL reaches AUROC 0.965 where text-only, audio-only, and fusion detectors stall below 0.69—the audio-only and fusion controls near chance—and—tellingly— scores lower on the saturated corpus, exactly as a detector that reasons about delivery rather than vocabulary memorization should. The result is a basis for on-device vishing defense that keeps raw audio local and stays robust when scam vocabulary shifts, together with a controlled benchmark for studying that robustness.
